claim: Following learning, increased coupling between spindle oscillations in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and ripple oscillations in the hippocampus is thought to underlie memory consolidation.
source: Following learning, increased coupling between spindle oscillations in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and ripple oscillations in the hippocampus is thought to underlie memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing literature in the introduction section, referencing the theoretical framework for ripple-spindle coupling in memory consolidation.

claim: Contextual fear conditioning increased ripple-spindle coupling in mice.
source: We found that contextual fear conditioning increased ripple-spindle coupling in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3, showing increased cross-correlation between ripple and spindle oscillations following fear conditioning.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells in either CA1 or mPFC eliminated the learning-induced increase in ripple-spindle coupling without affecting ripple or spindle incidence.
source: However, inhibition of PV+ cells in either CA1 or mPFC eliminated this learning-induced increase in ripple-spindle coupling without affecting ripple or spindle incidence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, demonstrating that CNO-mediated inhibition of PV+ cells prevented the increase in coupling while not changing the incidence of individual oscillations.

claim: Post-training inhibition of PV+ cells disrupted contextual fear memory consolidation.
source: Consistent with the hypothesized importance of ripple-spindle coupling in memory consolidation, post-training inhibition of PV+ cells disrupted contextual fear memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figures 4, 5, and 6, showing reduced freezing in CNO-treated mice compared to vehicle controls.

claim: Over 85% of endogenous PV+ cells were mCherry+, reflecting efficient infection rates.
source: Over 85% of endogenous PV+ cells were mCherry+, reflecting efficient infection rates (Figure 1b, n = 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from immunohistochemistry experiments shown in Figure 1b.

claim: More than 93% of mCherry+ cells expressed PV, indicating that infection was limited to the target cell type.
source: Moreover,>93% of mCherry+ cells expressed PV, indicating that infection was limited to the target cell type (Figure 1c, n = 10) (Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from immunohistochemistry experiments shown in Figure 1c and is consistent with previous literature (Sohal et al., 2009).

claim: CNO induced hyperpolarization of hM4Di-infected PV+ cells.
source: CNO induced hyperpolarization of hM4Di-infected PV+ cells, as bath application of CNO decreased firing rates of hM4Di-mCherry+, but not mCherry−, or mCherry+ cells in mice micro-infused with the control vector (Figure 1e; mixed-model permutation test, 1000 permutations, [hM4Di-mCherry+ versus hM4Di-mCherry- versus mCherry+] x [pre-CNO versus post-CNO]: p=0.001; individual cell firing rates pre- and post-CNO are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1d-e, demonstrating reduced firing rates in hM4Di-mCherry+ cells following CNO application.

claim: CNO decreased the input resistance of hM4Di-mCherry+ cells only.
source: Furthermore, CNO decreased the input resistance of hM4Di-mCherry+ cells only (Figure 1f; −80 pA current injection, two-way ANOVA, [hM4Di-mCherry+ versus hM4Di-mCherry- versus mCherry+] x [pre-CNO versus post-CNO]: F32,1 = 13.14, p=6.8×10−5, post hoc paired t-test with Bonferroni correction hM4Di-mCherry+ [pre-CNO versus post-CNO], t11 = 4.9, p=0.001, hM4Di-mCherry- [pre-CNO versus post-CNO], t9 = −2.3, p=0.12, mCherry+ [pre-CNO versus post-CNO], t12 = 0.67, p=1.0), consistent with the interpretation that activation of hM4Di opens inwardly-rectifying K+ channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1f, demonstrating changes in input resistance specific to hM4Di-expressing cells.

claim: Inhibiting PV+ cells in either the ACC or CA1 with CNO did not alter the incidence of ripples.
source: Inhibiting PV+ cells in either the ACC or CA1 with CNO did not alter the incidence of ripples (Figure 2c; Virus-ACC: n = 8 per group; two-way repeated measures ANOVA pre-training versus post-training x Vehicle (Veh) versus CNO; pre-training versus post-training F1,14 = 1.77, p=0.20; Veh versus CNO F1,14 = 0.0007, p=0.98; interaction F1,14 = 2.91, p=0.11; Virus-CA1: n = 8 per group; pre-training versus post-training F1,14 = 1.317, p=0.27; Veh versus CNO F1,14 = 3.63, p=0.077; interaction F1,14 = 0.10, p=0.76), consistent with previous reports using genetic manipulation of PV+ cells (Gan et al., 2017; Rácz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2c and is consistent with previous literature (Gan et al., 2017; Rácz et al., 2009).

claim: CNO-mediated inhibition of PV+ cells in either the ACC or CA1 did not alter the incidence of spindles.
source: CNO-mediated inhibition of PV+ cells in either the ACC or CA1 did not alter the incidence of spindles (Figure 2d; Virus-ACC: n = 8 per group; pre-training versus post-training F1,14 = 1.48, p=0.24; Veh versus CNO F1,14 = 2.25, p=0.16; interaction F1,14 = 3.54, p=0.081; Virus-CA1: n = 8 per group; pre-training versus post-training F1,14 = 0.039, p=0.85; Veh versus CNO F1,14 = 0.002, p=0.96; interaction F1,14 = 2.74, p=0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: CNO did not affect ripple or spindle amplitude.
source: Furthermore, CNO did not affect ripple or spindle amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b), induce seizure-like activity (i.e., high frequency oscillations) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d), nor alter sleep architecture (total NREM, NREM epoch duration) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: CNO did not induce seizure-like activity (i.e., high frequency oscillations).
source: Furthermore, CNO did not affect ripple or spindle amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b), induce seizure-like activity (i.e., high frequency oscillations) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d), nor alter sleep architecture (total NREM, NREM epoch duration) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: CNO did not alter sleep architecture (total NREM, NREM epoch duration).
source: Furthermore, CNO did not affect ripple or spindle amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b), induce seizure-like activity (i.e., high frequency oscillations) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d), nor alter sleep architecture (total NREM, NREM epoch duration) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e-f.

claim: A conditioning-dependent increase in ripple-spindle coupling was observed in vehicle-treated mice.
source: We computed the cross-correlation between ripple and spindle amplitudes and observed a conditioning-dependent increase in ripple-spindle coupling in vehicle-treated mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CNO-induced inhibition of PV+ cells post-training eliminated the conditioning-dependent increase in coupling.
source: CNO-induced inhibition of PV+ cells post-training eliminated the conditioning-dependent increase in coupling (Figure 3; Figure 3b: ACC: top; n = 8 per group; pre-training versus post-training F1,14 = 2.88, p=0.11; Veh versus CNO F1,14 = 0.15, p=0.70; interaction F1,14 = 6.68, p=0.022; post hoc Bonferroni's test, Veh pre-training versus Veh post-training p=0.018, CNO pre-training versus CNO post-training p>0.999; CA1: bottom; n = 8 per group; pre-training versus post-training F1,14 = 0.46, p=0.51; Veh versus CNO F1,14 = 0.09, p=0.77; interaction F1,14 = 8.42, p=0.012; post hoc Bonferroni's test, Veh pre-training versus Veh post-training p=0.048, CNO pre-training versus CNO post-training p=0.28; Figure 3c: ACC: top; n = 8 per group; Welch's t-test t9.24 = 2.46, p=0.035; Veh versus one one-sample t-test t7 = 2.59, p=0.036; CNO versus one one-sample t-test t7 = 0.17, p=0.87; CA1: bottom; Pre-training-normalized peak correlation coefficients, n = 8 per group; Mann-Whitney p=0.015; Veh versus one one-sample Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.008; CNO versus one one-sample Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.31).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3b-c.

claim: The peak levels of ripple-spindle coupling, during both Pre- and Post-training, were significantly higher than chance in all ACC- and CA1-infused mice.
source: The peak levels of ripple-spindle coupling, during both Pre- and Post-training, were significantly higher than chance in all ACC- and CA1-infused mice (an example is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing original correlations to shuffled data, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: CNO treatment had no effect on the conditioning-dependent increase in ripple-spindle coupling in mice micro-infused with the control vector (AAV-DIO-mCherry) into the ACC.
source: Importantly, CNO treatment had no effect on this conditioning-dependent increase in ripple-spindle coupling in mice micro-infused with the control vector (AAV-DIO-mCherry) into the ACC, indicating that the combination of hM4Di and CNO administration was necessary for the observed effects in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, demonstrating specificity of the hM4Di-CNO system.

claim: Following fear conditioning, PV+ cell activity was elevated in both CA1 and ACC (compared to untrained control mice).
source: Analysis of the activity-regulated gene, Fos, shows that following fear conditioning, PV+ cell activity was elevated in both CA1 and ACC (compared to untrained control mice), indicating that this population of cells is strongly activated by learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells in the ACC impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
source: Inhibition of PV+ cells in the ACC impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory, with CNO-treated mice freezing less compared to vehicle-treated controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4a, demonstrating reduced freezing in CNO-treated mice.

claim: Chronic, post-training suppression of PV+ cells in CA1 impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
source: Similarly, chronic, post-training suppression of PV+ cells in CA1 impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory (Figure 4a; ACC: Veh n = 6, CNO n = 8, Mann-Whitney test p=0.028; CA1: Veh n = 7, CNO n = 9, t-test t14 = 3.42, p=0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Inhibiting PV+ interneurons in either region immediately prior to testing did not affect freezing during test.
source: Inhibiting PV+ interneurons in either region immediately prior to testing did not affect freezing during test (Figure 4b; ACC: Veh n = 9, CNO n = 8, t-test t15 = 0.44, p=0.66; CA1: Veh n = 6, CNO n = 5, t-test t9 = 0.28, p=0.78), indicating that PV+ cell activity is not necessary for memory retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PV+ cell activity is not necessary for memory retrieval.
source: Inhibiting PV+ interneurons in either region immediately prior to testing did not affect freezing during test (Figure 4b; ACC: Veh n = 9, CNO n = 8, t-test t15 = 0.44, p=0.66; CA1: Veh n = 6, CNO n = 5, t-test t9 = 0.28, p=0.78), indicating that PV+ cell activity is not necessary for memory retrieval.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing no effect of PV+ cell inhibition on retrieval performance.

claim: Chronic (month-long) CNO treatment inhibited hM4Di-infected neurons without altering baseline neuronal excitability.
source: Using ex vivo patch-clamp experiments, we verified that chronic (month-long) CNO treatment inhibited hM4Di-infected neurons without altering baseline neuronal excitability (Figure 4c–e; Figure 4d: mCherry+ Veh n=14, CNO n = 20, mCherry- Veh n = 14, CNO n = 15, mixed-model permutation test, 1000 permutations, CNO versus Veh: p=0.77; Figure 4e: mCherry+ Veh n=14, CNO n = 20, mCherry- Veh n = 14, CNO n = 15, voltage clamp, mixed-model permutation test, 1000 permutations, CNO versus Veh: p=0.88).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4c-e.

claim: CNO water treatment reduced retrieval-induced activation of hM4Di-infected neurons in both CA1 and ACC.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the activity-regulated gene, Fos, confirmed that CNO water treatment reduced retrieval-induced activation of hM4Di-infected neurons in both CA1 and ACC (Figure 4f–h, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c; Figure 4g: Veh n = 4, CNO n = 5, t-test t7 = 1.37, p=0.21; Figure 4h: Veh n = 4, CNO n = 5, t-test t7 = 2.54, p=0.039).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4f-h and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Chronic CNO-induced suppression of ACC PV+ cell activity did not affect consolidation of tone fear conditioning.
source: In contrast to the effects observed in contextual fear conditioning, chronic CNO-induced suppression of ACC PV+ cell activity did not affect consolidation of tone fear conditioning (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d), suggesting that post-shock pain processing was not altered.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2d, serving as a control for pain processing effects.

claim: Chronic CNO-induced suppression of ACC PV+ cell activity did not alter general exploratory or anxiety-related behaviours.
source: Moreover, similar chronic CNO-induced suppression of ACC PV+ cell activity did not alter general exploratory or anxiety-related behaviours (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: Increases in ripple-spindle coupling were detected immediately following contextual fear conditioning, and not 7 or 14 days later.
source: However, in recording experiments, we detected increases in ripple-spindle coupling immediately following contextual fear conditioning, and not 7 or 14 days later (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CNO-induced suppression of PV+ cell activity in the ACC in the first, but not last, post-training week impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
source: CNO-induced suppression of PV+ cell activity in the ACC in the first, but not last, post-training week impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5a-b, demonstrating time-dependent effects of PV+ cell inhibition.

claim: Post-training suppression of PV+ interneuron activity in CA1 during the first, but not last, post-training week impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
source: Similarly, post-training suppression of PV+ interneuron activity in CA1 during the first, but not last, post-training week impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells in CA1 immediately following training impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
source: Inhibition of PV+ cells in CA1 impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory (Veh n = 7, CNO n = 10, t-test t15 = 2.75, p=0.015), consistent with a recent report (Ognjanovski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a and is consistent with previous literature (Ognjanovski et al., 2017).

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells in ACC immediately following training impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory.
source: Similarly, inhibition of PV+ cells in ACC impaired consolidation of contextual fear memory (Veh n = 12, CNO n = 16, t-test t26 = 3.10, p=0.0046).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Inhibiting PV+ interneurons in either region immediately prior to testing did not affect freezing during test 24 hr following training.
source: In contrast, inhibiting PV+ interneurons in either region immediately prior to testing did not affect freezing during test (Figure 6b; ACC: Veh n = 7, CNO n = 12, t-test t17 = 0.71, p=0.48; CA1: Veh n = 6, CNO n = 6, t-test t10 = 0.74, p=0.94), indicating that PV+ cell activity is not necessary for memory retrieval 24 hr following training.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Ripple-spindle coupling has been proposed to facilitate memory consolidation, and is increased following odor-reward learning.
source: Ripple-spindle coupling has been proposed to facilitate memory consolidation, and is increased following odor-reward learning (Mölle et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Mölle et al., 2009).

claim: Promoting ripple-spindle coupling enhances consolidation of an object-location memory.
source: Furthermore, promoting ripple-spindle coupling enhances consolidation of an object-location memory (Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Maingret et al., 2016).

claim: Contextual fear learning increased ripple-spindle coupling.
source: Here we found that contextual fear learning increased ripple-spindle coupling, and, furthermore, that chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells in the ACC or CA1 both eliminated this learning-induced increase in ripple-spindle coupling and impaired memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells in the ACC or CA1 both eliminated the learning-induced increase in ripple-spindle coupling and impaired memory consolidation.
source: Here we found that contextual fear learning increased ripple-spindle coupling, and, furthermore, that chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells in the ACC or CA1 both eliminated this learning-induced increase in ripple-spindle coupling and impaired memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data (Figure 3) and behavioral data (Figures 4-6).

claim: An average lag between ripple and spindle peak amplitude of ~70 ms was observed, consistent with ranges previously reported (40–244 ms).
source: We observed an average lag between ripple and spindle peak amplitude of ~70 ms, consistent with ranges previously reported (40–244 ms; e.g., [Peyrache et al., 2009; Phillips et al., 2012; Siapas and Wilson, 1998; Wang and Ikemoto, 2016; Wierzynski et al., 2009]).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of ripple-spindle timing and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: The observed lag between ripple and spindle peak amplitude suggests that these two events are more likely coordinated via multiple synapses.
source: This suggests that these two events are more likely coordinated via multiple synapses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing data and knowledge of synaptic transmission delays.

claim: ACC can modulate dorsal CA1 activity via thalamic regions, including nucleus reuniens.
source: For example, ACC can modulate dorsal CA1 activity via thalamic regions, including nucleus reuniens (e.g., [Varela et al., 2014; Xu and Südhof, 2013]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing anatomical pathways.

claim: mPFC neurons that project to the nucleus reuniens preferentially synapse onto hippocampus-projecting reuniens cells.
source: Interestingly, mPFC neurons that project to the nucleus reuniens preferentially synapse onto hippocampus-projecting reuniens cells (Vertes et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Vertes et al., 2007).

claim: A subset of neurons in the nucleus reuniens project to inhibitory interneurons in CA1.
source: In addition, a subset of neurons in the nucleus reuniens project to inhibitory interneurons in CA1 (Dolleman-Van der Weel and Witter, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Dolleman-Van der Weel and Witter, 2000).

claim: A group of nucleus reuniens cells has collaterals in both CA1 and mPFC, potentially coordinating activities between the two regions.
source: Furthermore, a group of nucleus reuniens cells also has collaterals in both CA1 and mPFC, potentially coordinating activities between the two regions (Varela et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Varela et al., 2014) and involves speculation about functional coordination.

claim: PV+ cells likely coordinate ripple-spindle coupling by facilitating synchronized spiking during ripples and spindles.
source: PV+ cells likely coordinate ripple-spindle coupling by facilitating synchronized spiking during ripples and spindles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and knowledge of PV+ cell function.

claim: In CA1 and mPFC, PV+ cell activity is phase-locked to ripples and spindles, respectively.
source: In CA1 and mPFC, PV+ cell activity is phase-locked to ripples (Klausberger et al., 2003) and spindles (Averkin et al., 2016; Hartwich et al., 2009; Peyrache et al., 2011), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In CA1, inhibition of PV+ cells disrupts phase-locked firing of PV+ cells to ripples, and ripple coherence.
source: In CA1, inhibition of PV+ cells disrupts phase-locked firing of PV+ cells to ripples, and ripple coherence (Gan et al., 2017; Stark et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Gan et al., 2017; Stark et al., 2014).

claim: PV+ cells act as a 'clocking mechanism' in circuits, ensuring that specific cell populations fire at appropriate times.
source: This is consistent with the proposed role of PV+ cells acting as a 'clocking mechanism' in circuits, ensuring that specific cell populations fire at appropriate times (Freund and Katona, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Freund and Katona, 2007).

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells in the ACC or CA1 did not affect baseline probability of ripple-spindle coupling, but prevented learning-induced increases in ripple-spindle coupling.
source: Inhibition of PV+ cells in the ACC or CA1 did not affect baseline probability of ripple-spindle coupling, but prevented learning-induced increases in ripple-spindle coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Following learning, PV+ cells show strong activation in both CA1 and ACC regions.
source: However, following learning we observed strong activation of PV+ cells in both regions, as well as a corresponding increase in the probability of ripple-spindle coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: CNO-mediated inhibition did not eliminate PV+ cell activity, but reduced it to pre-learning or home cage levels.
source: Importantly, CNO-mediated inhibition did not eliminate PV+ cell activity, but reduced it to pre-learning or home cage levels (as shown in our ex vivo and in vivo experiments).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data (Figure 1) and in vivo c-Fos data (Figure 4).

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells following learning should reduce ripple-spindle coupling to the levels that occur in the absence of training.
source: Therefore, we would expect that chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells following learning should not eliminate ripple-spindle coupling altogether, but instead, reduce it to the levels that occur in the absence of training, which is what we observed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and represents the authors' interpretation.

claim: Fear conditioning increases hippocampal network stability.
source: Consistent with this idea, fear conditioning increases hippocampal network stability (Donato et al., 2013), and chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells in CA1 blocks this learning-induced increase (Ognjanovski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Donato et al., 2013; Ognjanovski et al., 2017).

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells in CA1 blocks the learning-induced increase in hippocampal network stability.
source: Consistent with this idea, fear conditioning increases hippocampal network stability (Donato et al., 2013), and chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ cells in CA1 blocks this learning-induced increase (Ognjanovski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ognjanovski et al., 2017).

claim: When PV+ activity levels are driven below baseline levels via other techniques, there is an associated reduction in the probability of ripple-spindle coupling, even in the absence of learning.
source: Notably, when PV+ activity levels are driven below baseline levels via other techniques, there is an associated reduction in the probability of ripple-spindle coupling, even in the absence of learning (Phillips et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Phillips et al., 2012).

claim: The overall levels of PV+ cell activity regulate the probability of ripple-spindle coupling.
source: This suggests that the overall levels of PV+ cell activity regulate the probability of ripple-spindle coupling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and previous literature.

claim: Strong activation of PV+ cells during learning may increase coherence both within and across brain regions.
source: Accordingly, strong activation of PV+ cells during learning (Donato et al., 2013; Restivo et al., 2015; Ruediger et al., 2011) may increase coherence both within and across brain regions.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and previous literature (Donato et al., 2013; Restivo et al., 2015; Ruediger et al., 2011).

claim: Synchronous activity, such as ripple-spindle coupling, is particularly effective at driving inter-regional communication and plasticity required for consolidation.
source: Synchronous activity, such as ripple-spindle coupling, is particularly effective at driving inter-regional communication and plasticity required for consolidation (Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Igarashi, 2015; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Igarashi, 2015; Wang et al., 2010).

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cell activity in either the CA1 or the mPFC likely prevented the learning-induced increase in coupling by perturbing intra-regional synchrony of action potentials during ripples and spindles.
source: Therefore, inhibition of PV+ cell activity in either the CA1 or the mPFC likely prevented this learning-induced increase in coupling, by perturbing intra-regional synchrony of action potentials during ripples and spindles, and consequently, the coordination of inter-regional communication.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and represents the authors' mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Overall activity in ACC and CA1 are known to be important for retrieval of contextual fear memories.
source: Since overall activity in ACC and CA1 are known to be important for retrieval of contextual fear memories, these observations suggest that the activity of non-PV+ cells was not affected by our PV manipulations.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The activity of non-PV+ cells was not affected by PV manipulations.
source: Since overall activity in ACC and CA1 are known to be important for retrieval of contextual fear memories, these observations suggest that the activity of non-PV+ cells was not affected by our PV manipulations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of retrieval deficits and is supported by c-Fos data showing no change in mCherry- cells.

claim: The c-Fos levels in mCherry- cells in ACC and CA1 following CNO treatment were not altered.
source: Consistent with this, the c-Fos levels in mCherry- cells in these regions following CNO treatment were not altered.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Ripples are associated with simultaneous memory trace reactivation in the hippocampus and neocortex.
source: Ripples are associated with simultaneous memory trace reactivation in the hippocampus and neocortex (Peyrache et al., 2011; Peyrache et al., 2009; Schwindel and McNaughton, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Peyrache et al., 2011; Peyrache et al., 2009; Schwindel and McNaughton, 2011).

claim: Impaired ripple coherence following CA1 inhibition of PV+ cells likely reduced coordinated hippocampal output to the neocortex.
source: Therefore, impaired ripple coherence following CA1 inhibition of PV+ cells (Stark et al., 2014) likely reduced coordinated hippocampal output to the neocortex, and consequently decreased the probability of simultaneous memory trace reactivation in the neocortex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and previous literature (Stark et al., 2014).

claim: In the mPFC, memory trace reactivation is often followed by occurrence of spindles, and increased activation of local PV+ cells.
source: In the mPFC, memory trace reactivation is often followed by occurrence of spindles, and increased activation of local PV+ cells (Peyrache et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Peyrache et al., 2011).

claim: Increased activation of PV+ cells following memory trace reactivation is thought to favor the consolidation of recently modified synapses during memory reactivation, while suppressing interfering inputs to the neocortex.
source: This is thought to favor the consolidation of recently modified synapses during memory reactivation, while suppressing interfering inputs to the neocortex.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical understanding from previous literature.

claim: ACC inhibition of PV+ cells interfered with the timely occurrence of spindles following ripples/memory reactivation.
source: Since ACC inhibition of PV+ cells was sufficient to disrupt ripple-spindle coupling (without changing the overall incidence of spindles or ripples), this suggests that our manipulation interfered with the timely occurrence of spindles following ripples/memory reactivation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing disrupted coupling without changes in oscillation incidence.

claim: Inhibition of ACC PV+ cells likely prevented the strengthening of synapses in the neocortex that is necessary for memory consolidation.
source: Therefore, inhibition of ACC PV+ cells likely prevented the strengthening of synapses in the neocortex that is necessary for memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and represents the authors' mechanistic interpretation.

claim: PV+ cells are necessary for learning-associated increases in ripple-spindle coupling probability, and consequently, successful memory consolidation.
source: Our findings provide support for the idea that PV+ cells are necessary for learning-associated increases in ripple-spindle coupling probability, and consequently, successful memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study and is supported by the combined electrophysiology and behavioral data.

claim: The role of PV+ interneurons is likely similar during consolidation of appetitively-motivated tasks as well as aversively-motivated tasks.
source: Ripple-spindle coupling is also increased following odor-reward learning (Mölle et al., 2009), and therefore it seems plausible that the role of PV+ interneurons is similar during consolidation of appetitively-motivated (as well as aversively-motivated) tasks.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the current results and previous literature (Mölle et al., 2009).

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells may have increased lateral disinhibition and disrupted local circuit activity, in addition to disrupting global communication.
source: For example, it is possible that the effects of inhibition of PV+ cells outside of the sleep period (i.e., the ripple-spindle coupling window) could contribute to the consolidation deficits that we observed. Moreover, inhibition of PV+ cells may have increased lateral disinhibition and disrupted local circuit activity, in addition to disrupting global communication (i.e., ripple-spindle coupling).
evidence: This claim acknowledges alternative explanations for the observed effects.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells in either ACC or CA1 immediately following training impaired memory tested 24 hr later.
source: First, we found that inhibition of PV+ cells in either ACC or CA1 immediately following training impaired memory tested 24 hr later.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Activity in CA1, but not ACC, is critical for expression of contextual fear memory at 24 hr post-training.
source: Activity in CA1, but not ACC, is critical for expression of contextual fear memory at this time point (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).

claim: If PV manipulation only affected local activity, memory deficits would not be predicted following inhibition of ACC PV+ cells.
source: Therefore, if our manipulation of PV+ cells activity only affected local activity, we would not predict the memory deficits following inhibition of ACC PV+ cells.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the experimental results and established knowledge.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells had no effect on retrieval of contextual fear memories, tested either 24 hr or 28 days post-training.
source: Second, inhibition of PV+ cells had no effect on retrieval of contextual fear memories, tested either 24 hr or 28 days post-training, suggesting again that the overall local activity is relatively undisturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 4b and 6b.

claim: The PV manipulation is distinct from other manipulations that more profoundly impact pyramidal cell activity in ACC and CA1.
source: This reinforces the idea that our PV manipulation is distinct from other manipulations that more profoundly impact pyramidal cell activity in these regions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of retrieval deficits and represents the authors' interpretation.

claim: Increased activation in mCherry- cells in targeted regions following inhibition of PV+ interneurons was not observed.
source: Third, consistent with this, we did not observe increased activation in mCherry- cells in targeted regions following inhibition of PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The observed deficits are caused by disrupted global synchrony (i.e., ripple-spindle coupling).
source: Therefore, the more plausible explanation is that the observed deficits are caused by disrupted global synchrony (i.e., ripple-spindle coupling).
evidence: This claim represents the authors' interpretation based on the combined evidence.

claim: One advantage of the chemogenetic approach is that chemogenetic-induced inhibition does not completely eliminate the activity of infected cells.
source: One advantage of this approach is that chemogenetic-induced inhibition does not completely eliminate the activity of infected cells (e.g., compared to some forms of optogenetic silencing), and therefore is less likely to produce large-scale changes in overall circuit activity.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of chemogenetic versus optogenetic methods.

claim: A detectable increase in activation of mCherry- cells in either in vivo or ex vivo experiments was not observed.
source: Consistent with this, we did not observe a detectable increase in activation of mCherry- cells in either in vivo or ex vivo experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos and electrophysiology data.

claim: The PV manipulation did not produce broad changes in local field potential at theta or gamma frequencies.
source: This may also explain why our PV manipulation did not produce broad changes in local field potential at theta (Amilhon et al., 2015) or gamma (Sohal et al., 2009) frequencies, as previously observed using optogenetic silencing of PV+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the power spectrum analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-d and is contrasted with previous literature (Amilhon et al., 2015; Sohal et al., 2009).

claim: PV+ cells represent only a subpopulation of GABAergic interneurons in both ACC and CA1.
source: The absence of changes in the activity of non-infected neurons may also be related to the fact that PV+ cells represent only a subpopulation of GABAergic interneurons in both ACC and CA1 (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013; Rudy et al., 2011; Tremblay et al., 2016), and therefore it is plausible that non-infected cells in the circuit can still maintain homeostasis of spiking activity when the activity of PV+ cells is suppressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013; Rudy et al., 2011; Tremblay et al., 2016).

claim: Non-infected cells in the circuit can still maintain homeostasis of spiking activity when the activity of PV+ cells is suppressed.
source: The absence of changes in the activity of non-infected neurons may also be related to the fact that PV+ cells represent only a subpopulation of GABAergic interneurons in both ACC and CA1 (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013; Rudy et al., 2011; Tremblay et al., 2016), and therefore it is plausible that non-infected cells in the circuit can still maintain homeostasis of spiking activity when the activity of PV+ cells is suppressed.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and knowledge of circuit properties.

claim: Reducing PV-mediated inhibition could lead to disinhibition of other inhibitory cell types.
source: Moreover, reducing PV-mediated inhibition could lead to disinhibition of other inhibitory cell types (e.g., [Lovett-Barron et al., 2012]), thereby producing little overall change in excitation or inhibition.
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to previous literature (Lovett-Barron et al., 2012).

claim: Contextual fear learning increased the probability of ripple-spindle coupling.
source: In conclusion, here we showed that contextual fear learning increased the probability of ripple-spindle coupling.
evidence: This claim summarizes a main finding and is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data.

claim: Temporally correlated activities across brain regions are necessary for contextual fear memory consolidation.
source: These data indicate that temporally correlated activities across brain regions are necessary for contextual fear memory consolidation, and our study provides evidence for an integral role for PV+ cells in this process.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined electrophysiology and behavioral results.

claim: PV+ cells play an integral role in temporally correlated activities across brain regions necessary for memory consolidation.
source: These data indicate that temporally correlated activities across brain regions are necessary for contextual fear memory consolidation, and our study provides evidence for an integral role for PV+ cells in this process.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main conclusion and is supported by the combined experimental evidence.

claim: PV-Cre mice express Cre-recombinase only in PV+ cells.
source: To target PV+ interneurons in the ACC or CA1, we micro-infused an adeno-associated virus (AAV) that expresses the inhibitory Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD) hM4Di with a fluorescent reporter (mCherry) in a Cre-recombinase-dependent manner (AAV-DIO-hM4Di-mCherry) in mice expressing Cre-recombinase only in PV+ cells (PV-Cre mice) (Armbruster et al., 2007; Hippenmeyer et al., 2005; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on the genetic properties of the PV-Cre mouse line and is supported by citations.

claim: The AAV-DIO-hM4Di-mCherry virus expresses hM4Di-mCherry in a Cre-dependent manner.
source: To target PV+ interneurons in the ACC or CA1, we micro-infused an adeno-associated virus (AAV) that expresses the inhibitory Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD) hM4Di with a fluorescent reporter (mCherry) in a Cre-recombinase-dependent manner (AAV-DIO-hM4Di-mCherry) in mice expressing Cre-recombinase only in PV+ cells (PV-Cre mice) (Armbruster et al., 2007; Hippenmeyer et al., 2005; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim describes the viral vector design and is supported by citations.

claim: mCherry+ cells from both hM4Di- and control vector-infused mice exhibited much higher spiking rates than mCherry− cells across all current levels tested prior to CNO application.
source: mCherry+ cells from both hM4Di- and control vector-infused mice exhibited much higher spiking rates than mCherry− cells across all current levels tested prior to CNO application, verifying that infection was limited to fast-spiking PV+ interneurons (Klausberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1d and is consistent with previous literature (Klausberger et al., 2003).

claim: Infection was limited to fast-spiking PV+ interneurons.
source: mCherry+ cells from both hM4Di- and control vector-infused mice exhibited much higher spiking rates than mCherry− cells across all current levels tested prior to CNO application, verifying that infection was limited to fast-spiking PV+ interneurons (Klausberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electrophysiological properties of recorded cells and is supported by previous literature (Klausberger et al., 2003).

claim: There were no changes in the excitability of mCherry- cells following bath application of CNO.
source: There were no changes in the excitability of mCherry- cells following bath application of CNO.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1d-f.

claim: Pyramidal cells in ex vivo slices do not receive inhibitory input from PV+ cells at baseline.
source: This is likely because pyramidal cells in ex vivo slices do not receive inhibitory input from PV+ cells at baseline, and therefore inhibiting PV+ cells with bath application of CNO has no further effect on pyramidal cell excitability.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of slice physiology and represents the authors' interpretation.

claim: The effect of CNO-mediated inhibition is specific for hM4Di+ cells.
source: These experiments also demonstrate that the effect of our manipulation (i.e., CNO-mediated inhibition) is specific for hM4Di+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the ex vivo electrophysiology data showing selective effects on hM4Di-mCherry+ cells.

claim: Ripple-spindle coupling was previously found to increase following training in an odor-reward task.
source: Ripple-spindle coupling was previously found to increase following training in an odor-reward task (Mölle et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Mölle et al., 2009).

claim: Ripple-spindle coupling is observed most commonly during sleep.
source: Because ripple-spindle coupling is observed most commonly during sleep, we measured ripples (100–250 Hz) and spindles (12–15 Hz) during non-REM (NREM) periods in the pre- and post-training recording sessions using previously established criteria (Boyce et al., 2016; Klausberger et al., 2003; Phillips et al., 2012) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field and is supported by citations.

claim: Inhibiting CA3 PV+ cells disrupts ripple generation.
source: This finding contrasts with a previous study in which inhibiting CA3 PV+ cells disrupted ripple generation (Schlingloff et al., 2014), and suggests that PV+ cells may play region-specific roles in modulating ripple oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Schlingloff et al., 2014).

claim: PV+ cells may play region-specific roles in modulating ripple oscillations.
source: This finding contrasts with a previous study in which inhibiting CA3 PV+ cells disrupted ripple generation (Schlingloff et al., 2014), and suggests that PV+ cells may play region-specific roles in modulating ripple oscillations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the contrast between current results and previous literature (Schlingloff et al., 2014).

claim: An identical pattern of coupling disruption was observed using other measures of coupling (cross-correlation of ripple and spindle events and ripple-spindle joint occurrence rate).
source: An identical pattern was observed using other measures of coupling (cross-correlation of ripple and spindle events [Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–h] and ripple-spindle joint occurrence rate [Figure 2—figure supplement 1i]).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g-i.

claim: The baseline coupling likely reflected a significant, continuous communication between ACC and CA1.
source: This suggests that the baseline coupling still likely reflected a significant, continuous communication between ACC and CA1, but this level was dynamically modulated by fear learning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that baseline coupling was above chance levels.

claim: The baseline level of coupling was dynamically modulated by fear learning.
source: This suggests that the baseline coupling still likely reflected a significant, continuous communication between ACC and CA1, but this level was dynamically modulated by fear learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing increased coupling following fear conditioning.

claim: Intact PV+ cell activity in both ACC and CA1 is necessary for coordinating the enhanced hippocampal-neocortical communication following learning.
source: Our findings that post-conditioning inhibition of PV+ cells in either the ACC or CA1 eliminated ripple-spindle coupling indicates that intact PV+ cell activity in both regions is necessary for coordinating the enhanced hippocampal-neocortical communication following learning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that inhibition in either region disrupts coupling.

claim: The post-conditioning increase in coupling between ripple and ACC delta oscillations was eliminated by inhibition of PV+ cells in either the ACC or CA1.
source: Similar to the effects of inhibiting PV+ cells on disrupting ripple-spindle coupling, we observed that the post-conditioning increase in coupling between ripple and ACC delta oscillations was eliminated by inhibition of PV+ cells in either the ACC or CA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: Inhibiting PV+ cells did not affect the time lag between baseline ripple and spindle, or between ripple and delta, peak correlation.
source: Importantly, inhibiting PV+ cells did not affect the time lag between baseline ripple and spindle, or between ripple and delta, peak correlation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by timing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e-f.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ cells prevents learning-induced increases in the probability of coupling of hippocampal-neocortical oscillations, but not the baseline interactions.
source: Thus, inhibition of PV+ cells prevents learning-induced increases in the probability of coupling of hippocampal-neocortical oscillations, but not the baseline interactions.
evidence: This claim summarizes the electrophysiology findings and is supported by the data in Figure 3.

claim: Activation of the activity-regulated gene Fos in PV+ cells was elevated following fear conditioning in both CA1 and ACC.
source: Analysis of the activity-regulated gene, Fos, shows that following fear conditioning, PV+ cell activity was elevated in both CA1 and ACC (compared to untrained control mice), indicating that this population of cells is strongly activated by learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: PV+ cells are strongly activated by learning.
source: Analysis of the activity-regulated gene, Fos, shows that following fear conditioning, PV+ cell activity was elevated in both CA1 and ACC (compared to untrained control mice), indicating that this population of cells is strongly activated by learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the c-Fos data and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Results are consistent with previous studies showing strong activation of inhibitory interneurons following learning.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies showing strong activation of inhibitory interneurons following learning (Pi et al., 2013; Sparta et al., 2014), and, specifically, PV+ cells following fear conditioning (Donato et al., 2013; Restivo et al., 2015; Ruediger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Pi et al., 2013; Sparta et al., 2014; Donato et al., 2013; Restivo et al., 2015; Ruediger et al., 2011).
